## Conversation summary (from export)

<conversation_overview>
The person is building a Python application for an AI Engineer coding challenge, with a submission deadline of November 1. The task required a terminal program that captures microphone and system audio simultaneously, transcribes Armenian speech, translates it to English, and identifies speakers, all running locally on an Intel Core i5-8250U laptop with 8 GB RAM and no GPU, within a 5-second latency requirement. The person explicitly wanted to be actively involved in engineering decisions, understand every component, and approach the work through measured experiments rather than having Claude generate a complete solution immediately.

Work proceeded through a structured sequence: initial planning and risk identification (documented in PLAN.md), speech-recognition model selection (settling on omniASR-CTC-300M-v2 in int8 precision after benchmarking against Whisper variants, achieving ~6.3% character error rate with ~1.5s latency on 6-second phrases), translation model selection (NLLB-200-distilled-600M via CTranslate2 in int8 with beam size 1, validated through blind human ratings), audio capture implementation (WASAPI loopback via PyAudioWPatch, resampled with soxr), a phrase-segmentation module, and speaker identification (WeSpeaker ResNet34-LM via sherpa-onnx). All major decisions, experiments, and their quantitative results were logged in DECISIONS.md and EXPERIMENTS.md, with raw data saved as JSON/JSONL files.

Significant debugging occurred around live-session issues: Armenian-only CTC decoding was added after the model drifted into other scripts and caused translation hallucinations; a translation repetition-loop bug was fixed with length caps and n-gram constraints; a confidence-based filter (threshold 0.80) was added to flag unclear speech rather than mistranslate it, validated by replaying recorded audio against what the person actually said; and speaker identification went through several iterations (centering embeddings against a prior mean, threshold tuning across three labelled recordings, and a "confirm new speaker" rule) before settling on balanced accuracy as the evaluation metric, since the initial F-score metric rewarded merging speakers when one dominated a recording. The person provided ground-truth labels for speaker-identification recordings and corrected several of Claude's assumptions (e.g., clarifying that silence during a test was intentional, not a capture failure). A HANDOVER.md file was maintained across two work sessions to preserve full context, including exact next steps, open decisions, and a day-by-day plan through the deadline (environment setup, speaker ID refinement and real-call testing, README/TESTS.md writing, full rehearsal, and chat-history export). The person consistently prioritized working code and reliability over additional model comparisons once behind-schedule pressure emerged, and asked Claude to verify every claim with actual measurements on their hardware rather than relying on published benchmarks or assumptions.

</conversation_overview>

On other systems, use the equivalent.\n\n- Let the user pick the input devices, for example from a printed device list or by command-line flags.\n\n- **Armenian transcription.** Turn spoken Armenian into Armenian text.\n\n- **English translation.** Translate each transcribed segment into English.\n\n- **Speaker identification.**\n\n- Everything from the microphone is labelled Me.\n\n- On the system-audio side, different people are told apart and labelled Speaker 1, Speaker 2 and so on. Isolate modules with clear inputs and outputs**\n\nWhen a codebase grows, take one module or workflow, define exactly what goes in and what comes out, and develop and test it in a separate chat. Measure, don****'****t guess**\n\nBuild a small evaluation set early (e.g. a few short Armenian recordings with the correct text) and measure what matters: error rate, latency, speaker labels. Compare models with numbers, not impressions.\n\n## **6. Give little, but the right context**\n\nDo not dump many files into a chat. Too much context makes the AI worse: it loses focus and starts to hallucinate. When a chat gets long, write a short handover (goal, current state, decisions, next step), start a new chat with it, and only go back to the old one to look something up.\n\n## **7. **Inference speed and CPU deployment:**
```
- Per-token decoding throughput is about 73 tokens/sec and is essentially the same across Whisper zero-shot, simple fine-tuning, and full fine-tuning, since they share the Whisper-large-v3 decoder.
- The gains come from the adapted tokenizer, which produces shorter sequences. Full fine-tuning has a global median latency of about 503 ms per utterance versus about 785 ms for Whisper zero-shot, roughly a 1.6× speedup.
- Gains vary by script. The speedup is 1.59× for Latin and 1.75× for Cyrillic, but only 1.16× for Brahmic scripts.
- Benchmarks were run in FP16 with batch size 1 on a single A100-80GB GPU. The paper says nothing about CPU deployment.
```

`content` (raw text):

````
# PLAN.md: Live Armenian Transcription → English Translation

Status: **draft for review**. Nothing is installed or implemented yet.
Target machine: Windows laptop, Intel Core i5-8250U (4 cores / 8 threads, 15 W, no GPU), 8 GB RAM.

---

## 1. Goal

A Python terminal program that captures **microphone + system audio at the same time**, transcribes spoken **Armenian**, translates it to **English**, and prints one line block per phrase with **time, speaker, HY text, EN text**. It must do this within **≤ 5 s of the end of each phrase**, using **local models only**.

### 1.1 Mandatory requirements (from the brief)

| # | Requirement | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | Capture mic and system output **simultaneously** | Windows: WASAPI loopback. No virtual cable needed, and the user still hears the call. |
| R2 | User can **pick the input devices** | `--list-devices`, `--mic <id>`, `--loopback <id>` |
| R3 | Armenian speech → Armenian text | Low-resource language. This is the main quality risk. |
| R4 | Each segment translated to English | |
| R5 | Mic is always labelled **Me** | Comes from the source, so no model is needed. |
| R6 | System-audio speakers labelled **Speaker 1, 2, …**, with labels **stable for the session** | Needs online speaker clustering. |
| R7 | Live terminal output: `[hh:mm:ss] Speaker`, `HY: …`, `EN: …` | |
| C1 | **≤ 5 s** from end of phrase to EN line | Measured per segment and logged. |
| C2 | Transcription, translation and speaker ID all **local** | No cloud APIs at runtime. |
| C3 | Python, runs on **this laptop** | |
| C4 | Models chosen deliberately and justified in the README | Based on our own measurements. |

### 1.2 Deliverables
- Git repo containing the source code, a `README.md` (setup + audio setup, model choices + alternatives, architecture, limitations, improvements), and a `chats/` folder with **every** Claude session exported in full, one `.md` per session.
- No model weights, audio recordings or keys in git. `.gitignore` takes care of this from the first commit.
- Supporting docs (per the guidelines): `DECISIONS.md` (decision log), `TESTS.md` (requirement-driven test list), and a project-rules file.

### 1.3 Success criteria (what the interview checks)
1. It starts and runs during a live call with ≥ 2 Armenian speakers on the call side.
2. Armenian is recognised well enough that the English is **understandable**.
3. Each phrase stays **under 5 s** from end of phrase to EN line. We print the measured latency so it can be verified.
4. Speakers are **kept apart**, and labels don't swap mid-session.
5. Code has clean separation: audio / VAD / ASR / translation / speakers / output.
6. The README is honest about limits, and every model choice is backed by numbers from our eval set.
7. The chat history shows planning, measurement and steering.

Out of scope (per the brief, so we won't build it): GUI, installer, echo cancellation, naming speakers, cross-session memory, saving transcripts, non-Armenian input. Spare time goes into **reliability**.

---

## 2. Components (each independently testable)

| Module | Input | Output | Standalone test |
|---|---|---|---|
| `audio_capture` | device ids | stream of `(source, t_start, float32 16 kHz mono chunk)` | Record 10 s from both sources to WAV files. Both are clean, with no dropouts, and you still hear the call. |
| `vad_segmenter` | chunks for one source | `Segment(source, t_start, t_end, audio)` emitted at end of phrase | Feed a WAV with known pauses and check that segment boundaries are within ±0.3 s. Also enforce a max segment length. |
| `asr` | `Segment.audio` | Armenian text (+ timing) | Run on the eval set to get WER/CER, real-time factor and peak RAM. |
| `translate` | Armenian text | English text (+ timing) | Run on reference HY sentences to get readable EN and ms/sentence. |
| `speakers` | loopback segment audio | `"Speaker N"` | Feed labelled multi-speaker clips to measure label purity and the number of speakers created. |
| `pipeline` | segments from both sources | `Result(time, label, hy, en, latency)` | Replay pre-recorded WAVs as if live and check per-segment latency. |
| `output` | `Result` | formatted terminal lines | Unit test of the formatting. |
| `main` / CLI | flags | running app | Manual end-to-end test on a real call. |

Every module has one job, clear I/O, and fails loudly (no silent fallbacks).

---

## 3. Proposed minimal architecture

```
 Mic (WASAPI)  ──► capture thread ──► VAD segmenter (source=Me) ──┐
                                                                   ├─► segment queue ─► ONE worker:
 Loopback      ──► capture thread ──► VAD segmenter (source=Call)─┘     1. ASR (hy)
 (WASAPI)                                                               2. speaker ID (Call only)
                                                                        3. MT hy→en
                                                                        4. print + latency
```

Design choices and why:
- **WASAPI loopback** (e.g. `PyAudioWPatch` or `soundcard`). It captures exactly what plays on the output device, without a virtual cable. To verify in Spike 1: does it work with your default device and call app?
- **Resample to 16 kHz mono** at capture time, since all candidate models expect it.
- **Silero VAD per source**. A phrase ends after ~500–700 ms of silence. We also **force-cut at ~8–10 s** so a long monologue can't blow the latency budget.
- **One processing worker**, not one per source. The CPU has only 4 real cores. Running two model inferences in parallel would make both slower, and it would double RAM. Segments are processed in order of their end time.
- **Speaker ID only on the loopback side**, using a speaker-embedding model plus **online centroid clustering** (cosine similarity: assign to the nearest centroid above a threshold, otherwise create a new speaker). This is language-independent, so Armenian doesn't matter here. Segments shorter than a minimum duration don't create a new speaker.
- **Shared session clock** (monotonic, starting at program start) so timestamps from both sources line up.
- All model calls use **int8 CPU inference** (CTranslate2 / ONNX) where it's available.

### 3.1 Latency budget (end of phrase → EN line ≤ 5 s)

| Stage | Budget |
|---|---|
| VAD end-of-speech wait | 0.5–0.7 s |
| ASR (for a ≤ 8 s phrase) | ≤ 2.5 s |
| Speaker embedding | ≤ 0.3 s |
| Translation | ≤ 0.7 s |
| Queue wait + overhead | ≤ 0.8 s |
| **Total** | **≤ 5 s** |

The queue term is the hidden risk. If Me and a Speaker finish phrases at the same moment, the second one waits for the first one's whole pipeline. So in practice **ASR + MT has to be well under ~2 s per phrase**.

### 3.2 RAM budget (8 GB total)
Windows + call app (+ browser) will likely take 4–5 GB, which leaves **~3 GB for our models**. Rough sizes, to be measured: a large-v3-size ASR in int8 is ~1.5–2 GB, NLLB-600M int8 is ~0.6–1 GB, a speaker embedding model is < 0.1 GB, and VAD is tiny.

---

## 4. Model candidates (to be measured, not assumed)

### 4.1 ASR, the biggest risk

| Candidate | Size | What's known for Armenian | CPU concern |
|---|---|---|---|
| Whisper large-v3 (zero-shot) | 1.55 B | CER ≈ 14–16 % on FLEURS / Common Voice (reported on the BuzzASR card) | Probably too slow on this CPU |
| Whisper large-v3-turbo | ~0.8 B | Armenian quality **unverified** | Faster decoder, so a likely middle ground |
| **BuzzASR/armenian** (full fine-tune of large-v3, MIT) | 1.55 B | Self-reported CER 2.3 % combined (FLEURS WER 11.9 %). Big improvement, but Common Voice is partly in-domain. | Same size as large-v3. Needs a CTranslate2 conversion, and speed is unknown. |
| Whisper small/medium + community fine-tunes | 0.24–0.77 B | Reported WERs of 40–75 %, self-evaluated | Fast, but probably too inaccurate |
| Meta Omnilingual ASR (CTC 300M / 1B) | 0.3–1 B | Covers ~1600 languages. Armenian support and quality **to verify**. | Non-autoregressive (single pass), so potentially much faster |
| Meta MMS-1b-all (CTC, language adapters) | 1 B | Armenian adapter **to verify**. Older model. | Single pass |

Caveat: CTC models usually output no punctuation or casing, and that may hurt translation. We'll test it.

### 4.2 Translation

| Candidate | Notes |
|---|---|
| NLLB-200 distilled 600M (`hye_Armn → eng_Latn`) | Strong low-resource coverage, and CTranslate2 int8 versions exist. License is CC-BY-NC, fine for a challenge but noted in the README. |
| NLLB-200 distilled 1.3B | Better quality, about 2× slower. Only if the budget allows. |
| Opus-MT hy→en (Marian) | Very small and fast. Existence and quality **to verify**. |
| Whisper `task=translate` | Rejected for now. We need both HY and EN, so it would mean two decodes. |

### 4.3 Speaker embeddings
SpeechBrain ECAPA-TDNN (VoxCeleb), WeSpeaker ResNet34 (ONNX, e.g. via sherpa-onnx), or pyannote embedding (gated on Hugging Face). The full pyannote 3.x diarization pipeline is offline and heavy on CPU, so we don't need it. Our VAD segments plus clustering are enough.

---

## 5. Biggest technical risks

| # | Risk | Likelihood / impact | Mitigation | Tested in |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| K1 | **No ASR model is both accurate enough and fast enough on the i5-8250U** | High / critical | Measure early. Options: int8, beam size 1, turbo or CTC models, shorter max segments, fine-tuned large-v3 if it's fast enough. | Spike 3 |
| K2 | **Latency > 5 s when both sources speak at once**, or after long phrases | Medium / high | Single worker with ordered queue, max segment length, per-stage timing log, keep ASR+MT ≪ 2.5 s | Spike 6 |
| K3 | **CPU thermal throttling / power mode** (15 W laptop CPU) makes the interview run slower than the tests | Medium / high | Benchmark under sustained load (10+ min), plugged in, "Best performance" mode. Set the thread count explicitly. | Spikes 3 and 6 |
| K4 | **Speaker confusion**: call-codec audio, short utterances, similar voices, threshold sensitivity, labels splitting or merging | Medium / high | Minimum duration for new speakers, threshold tuned on our own clips, centroid update, test with ≥ 3 real voices through a real call | Spike 5 |
| K5 | **Call-audio quality** (Opus codec, noise) is worse than clean benchmark audio | High / medium | Eval set includes clips recorded **through a real call** via loopback | Spikes 2 and 3 |
| K6 | **RAM pressure** with a call app open → swapping → latency spikes | Medium / high | Measure peak RAM with the call app running. Prefer int8 and smaller models. | Spike 3 |
| K7 | **Translation of imperfect ASR text** is unreadable | Medium / medium | Evaluate MT on ASR output, not only on reference text | Spike 4 |
| K8 | **Overlapping speech** or two speakers in one segment | Medium / low–medium | Documented limitation. Short max segment helps. | Spike 5 |
| K9 | **Speakers instead of headphones**: the mic picks up the call → duplicate "Me" lines | Medium / medium | Echo is out of scope, so use headphones in the interview and document it | Spike 1 |
| K10 | Windows audio quirks: loopback device sample rate (48 kHz stereo), device ids changing, exclusive mode | Medium / medium | Device listing tool, resampling, test with the actual call app | Spike 1 |
| K11 | Model claims (AI or model cards) are wrong or don't apply | Medium / medium | Verify every model on our own eval set before deciding | Spikes 3–5 |

---

## 6. Feasibility-first order (milestones)

Each spike has a **pass criterion** and a **decision gate**. We commit after every working step. Hours add up to roughly 20.

| # | Milestone | ~h | Pass criterion / output |
|---|---|---|---|
| M0 | Repo, `.gitignore`, plan, DECISIONS.md, TESTS.md, project rules | 1 | Reviewed plan, first commit |
| M1 | **Spike 1: audio capture**: list devices, record mic + loopback simultaneously to WAV | 2 | Both WAVs intelligible, no dropouts over 60 s, you still hear the call, sample-rate handling correct |
| M2 | **Eval set**: 15–20 short Armenian clips (3–8 s), ≥ 3 voices, with typed reference text. Some clips recorded via a real call. Optionally add FLEURS hy_am samples. Audio stays out of git. | 1.5 | `eval/manifest.csv` with path, speaker, reference text |
| M3 | **Spike 3: ASR benchmark**: 3–4 candidates, CER/WER, real-time factor, peak RAM, sustained-load run | 4 | **Gate:** pick a model with ASR time ≤ ~2 s for a 5 s clip and the best CER. If none qualifies, revisit segment length, model size or approach before going further. |
| M4 | **Spike 4: translation benchmark** on references *and* on ASR output | 1.5 | ≤ 0.7 s per sentence; you judge whether the EN is understandable |
| M5 | **Spike 5: speaker ID** offline on labelled clips: embeddings + online clustering | 2.5 | Same person → same label in ≥ 90 % of segments ≥ 1.5 s, no label explosion, threshold chosen from data |
| M6 | **Walking skeleton**: live mic → VAD → ASR → MT → terminal, then add loopback, then speakers | 3 | Live output for both sources, latency printed per line |
| M7 | **Latency and robustness tuning** under realistic load (call app open, 15-minute run, simultaneous speech) | 2.5 | ≥ 95 % of segments ≤ 5 s, no crashes, no memory growth |
| M8 | README, limitations, chat export, **interview rehearsal** with real people on a call | 2 | Someone else can follow the README. A full rehearsal passes. |

Rule from the guidelines: if something fails three times, go back to the last working commit and narrow it down.

---

## 7. Testing and measurement

- **Accuracy:** CER (primary, more stable for Armenian morphology) and WER on the eval set, with normalisation (punctuation and case removed) defined in code.
- **Latency:** per-segment timestamps for `t_phrase_end`, `t_asr_done`, `t_mt_done` and `t_printed`, logged to the console in debug mode, with p50/p95 reported.
- **Speed:** real-time factor = processing time / audio duration, measured cold and after 10 minutes of warm, sustained load.
- **RAM:** peak RSS per model and for the whole app with the call app open.
- **Speakers:** label purity and number of speakers created vs. true number, on labelled clips and on the live rehearsal.
- **Requirement checklist** in `TESTS.md`, derived from R1–R7 and C1–C4, not from the code.

---

## 8. Open questions for you

1. **Call app for the interview**: Zoom, Google Meet, Teams, Telegram? In a browser or the desktop app? This affects which output device the audio goes to and the audio quality.
2. **Headphones or speakers?** Echo is out of scope. I'd suggest headphones so the mic doesn't pick up the call.
3. **Armenian variety**: Eastern Armenian only, as I assume? Do you expect some English words or code-switching (common in tech talk)?
4. **Accuracy vs. latency**: if the most accurate model only fits by cutting phrases at ~6 s, is that acceptable? Or do you prefer a smaller model with complete phrases?
5. **Eval data**: can you record a few friends or family (≥ 3 voices) reading short sentences, ideally once through a real call? Consent stays with them, and audio stays local.
6. **Environment**: is Python already installed (which version)? Git? How much free disk space do you have (models need ~3–6 GB)?
7. **Power**: will the laptop be plugged in during the interview? Are you OK with switching to the "Best performance" power mode?
8. **Python packaging preference**: plain `venv` + `requirements.txt` (my suggestion for simplicity), or `uv`/`conda`?
````

I've saved `PLAN.md` in your project folder. I didn't install, download or implement anything.

**The main risk is the speech-recognition model on your processor.** The Armenian accuracy figures below are what the model publishers report; I haven't tested anything yet. Nobody seems to have published speeds for laptop processors without a GPU, so the speed concerns are my own estimates, and measuring them is the first real test in the plan.
- **Whisper large-v3, unmodified:** it gets about 14–16% of characters wrong in Armenian, and it's probably too slow on your laptop.
- **BuzzASR/armenian:** a version of large-v3 retrained for Armenian. Its makers report about 2.3% of characters wrong, so far more accurate. But it's the same size as large-v3, so it's probably just as slow.
- **Small community Whisper models trained for Armenian:** they report about 40–75% of words wrong, which is likely unusable.
- **Meta's Omnilingual ASR and MMS:** they process audio in one pass, so they may be much faster. Whether they handle Armenian, and how well, still needs checking.

**The 5-second limit is tighter than it looks.** Waiting to detect that a phrase has ended already takes about 0.6 seconds. If you and a call participant finish speaking at the same moment, the second phrase waits for the first to be fully processed. So recognition plus translation has to take well under about 2 seconds per phrase.

**Proposed architecture:**
- **Audio:** a standard Windows feature called WASAPI loopback captures what plays through your speakers or headphones. No virtual audio cable is needed, and you still hear the call.
- **Splitting into phrases:** each audio source (your mic and the call) is split into phrases when a pause is detected. Long monologues are force-cut so they don't delay the output.
- **Processing:** a single worker handles one phrase at a time, so two models never compete for your 4 cores. Each phrase goes through recognition, then speaker identification (call side only), then translation.
- **Speaker identification:** each call-side phrase gets a "voice fingerprint", and similar fingerprints are grouped as the conversation goes. This doesn't depend on the language.

**Order of work:** first audio capture, then a set of 15–20 short Armenian recordings with typed transcripts for testing, then speed and accuracy tests of the recognition models. That test is a decision point: if no model is both fast and accurate enough, we rethink before building anything else. After that come translation, speaker identification, a bare end-to-end version, and then tuning and the README. The plan has about 20 hours of work, with a pass criterion for each step.

**Questions for you (also in section 8):**
1. Which call app will the interview use (Zoom, Meet, Teams…), and in a browser or the desktop app?
2. Will you use headphones? I recommend them, because the mic would otherwise pick up the call.
3. Is it Eastern Armenian only? Should we expect some English words mixed in?
4. If the most accurate model only fits by cutting phrases at about 6 seconds, is that acceptable? Or do you prefer a smaller model and complete phrases?
5. Can you record at least 3 different voices for the test set, ideally some through a real call?
6. Is Python installed, and which version? Is Git installed? How much free disk space do you have? Models need about 3–6 GB.
7. Will the laptop be plugged in, with Windows' "Best performance" power mode on? A 15 W laptop processor slows down noticeably on battery or when it heats up.
8. Are you OK with a plain Python virtual environment (venv) and a `requirements.txt` file?

```
The discussion doesn't mention Windows, CPU, or ONNX. It covers running the model with Hugging Face `transformers` and avoiding the fairseq2 dependency.

- **Opener (aadel4, Mar 15):** Because the model is based on Wav2Vec2.0, it could replace existing Wav2Vec2.0 pipelines, but only if it runs without fairseq2.
- **Conversions:** The author converted the 300M and 1B CTC (V1 and V2) and SSL checkpoints to the native Hugging Face `Wav2Vec2ForCTC` format.
- **Usage:** The converted models can run inference with standard `transformers` in a few lines of code, with no fairseq2 required.
- **Limitations:** The 3B+ variants weren't converted due to GPU limitations.
- **Resources:** The author linked the converted 300M and 1B models and open-sourced the conversion code on GitHub, inviting contributions.
```

</details>

<details><summary>Tool result: <code></code></summary>

<sub>for tool_use id `toolu_01P5rEupE6PmbYhh4Q9CXuWU`</sub>

```
The thread doesn't settle the padding question or discuss encoder cost directly.

- **The original poster's assumption:** They believed Whisper pads audio shorter than 30 seconds to 30 seconds, so all files should take about the same time. Their benchmark showed otherwise.
- **The reply:** kvrban said the reverse is true: "audio files longer than 30s are processed in 30s chunks." They added that nothing changes for audio below 30 seconds, while noting this was their own partial understanding.
- **The follow-up:** The original poster said the paper only explicitly describes chunking longer audio, but they found code in faster-whisper that applies `pad_or_trim` to each segment, targeting `nb_max_frames`. This suggests padding to 30 seconds does occur, though the thread doesn't explain how that affects runtime.
- **Workarounds:** None are given. The page links to "Support for variable size chunks #54" and an openai/whisper discussion about padding masks, but their content isn't included here, so I can't say whether they offer a fix.
```

</details>

```
## 8. Open questions for you

1. **Call app for the interview**: Zoom, Google Meet, Teams, Telegram? In a browser or the desktop app? This affects which output device the audio goes to and the audio quality.
2. **Headphones or speakers?** Echo is out of scope. I'd suggest headphones so the mic doesn't pick up the call.
3. **Armenian variety**: Eastern Armenian only, as I assume? Do you expect some English words or code-switching (common in tech talk)?
4. **Accuracy vs. latency**: if the most accurate model only fits by cutting phrases at ~6 s, is that acceptable? Or do you prefer a smaller model with complete phrases?
5. **Eval data**: can you record a few friends or family (≥ 3 voices) reading short sentences, ideally once through a real call? Consent stays with them, and audio stays local.
6. **Environment**: is Python already installed (which version)? Git? How much free disk space do you have (models need ~3–6 GB)?
7. **Power**: will the laptop be plugged in during the interview? Are you OK with switching to the "Best performance" power mode?
8. **Python packaging preference**: plain `venv` + `requirements.txt` (my suggestion for simplicity), or `uv`/`conda`?
```

````
# DECISIONS.md: Decision log

Each entry: **context → decision → reasons → status**. "Proposed" entries are waiting for review. Facts marked *(self-reported)* come from a model card or paper and haven't been measured by us yet.

---

## D-001 · Capture system audio with WASAPI loopback (no virtual cable)
- **Context:** The call app isn't fixed (Zoom, Meet, …). The user must still hear the call.
- **Decision:** Capture the Windows **output device** through WASAPI loopback, plus the mic as a normal input. Both devices can be picked from the CLI.
- **Reasons:** Works with any app that plays through that device. It's built into Windows, so nothing to install system-wide, and playback isn't affected.
- **Status:** Accepted in principle. Verified in Spike 1 (audio).

## D-002 · Headphones during the demo
- **Decision:** Assume headphones. No echo cancellation (out of scope per the brief).
- **Status:** Accepted.

## D-003 · `venv` + `requirements.txt`, pinned versions
- **Status:** Accepted.

## D-004 · Environment check before any install
- **Context:** The tool I use on your laptop runs in a **Linux VM** with your project folder mounted (it reports Python 3.10 / Linux). It cannot see your Windows Python or Git, so its output says nothing about your actual setup.
- **Decision:** You run the checks in **Windows PowerShell** and paste the output:
  ```powershell
  python --version
  py -0p
  where.exe python
  python -c "import platform, struct; print(platform.platform(), struct.calcsize('P')*8, 'bit')"
  git --version
  ```
  We need **64-bit** Python 3.12, since prebuilt wheels for CTranslate2/ONNX Runtime are 64-bit only, and a working `git`.
- **Status:** Waiting for output.

## D-005 · ASR candidate verification (desk research, 2026-10-25)

| Candidate | Armenian support | License | Runs natively on Windows? | Size / compute | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Whisper large-v3** via faster-whisper | Yes (`hy` is a built-in language). Zero-shot CER ≈ 14–16 % *(self-reported, BuzzASR card)* | MIT (model and faster-whisper) | Yes: `pip install faster-whisper` (CTranslate2, no PyTorch, no FFmpeg) | 1.55 B params. Int8 on CPU. ~3 GB download. | **Test first** (baseline + speed gate) |
| **Whisper large-v3-turbo** via faster-whisper | Same tokenizer and languages. Armenian quality **unknown** | MIT | Yes | ~0.8 B. Same 32-layer encoder, only 4 decoder layers | Test alongside large-v3 |
| **BuzzASR/armenian** (Whisper large-v3, fully fine-tuned) | Monolingual Armenian. CER 2.3 % combined, FLEURS WER 11.9 % *(self-reported; Common Voice partly in-domain)* | MIT | Only in Transformers format (3.09 GB F16). No CTranslate2 build, no `tokenizer.json`. **Extended vocabulary: 53,474 tokens vs 51,866 in large-v3**, so conversion to faster-whisper must be tested. | Same compute as large-v3 | Test **only if large-v3 is fast enough** |
| **MMS-1b-all** (Meta, CTC + language adapters) | Yes, `hye` adapter. Community ONNX spot-check: CER 0.03 on one FLEURS sentence (not a benchmark) | **CC-BY-NC-4.0** (non-commercial) | Yes, via `transformers` + PyTorch CPU, or a community ONNX export (int8 base ≈ 1 GB) | 1 B. **Cost scales with clip length** (no 30 s window) | Fallback / speed alternative |
| **Omnilingual ASR CTC 300M / 1B** (Meta) | **Not confirmed** from the sources I could read | Apache-2.0 | **No:** the official stack uses fairseq2, which has "no native support for Windows" (WSL only). Unofficial Transformers conversions exist. | 0.3 / 1 B | Deferred |
| Small community Whisper fine-tunes (tiny/small) | Self-reported 40–75 % WER on their own validation sets | Various | Yes | Small | Dropped: too inaccurate |

**Key technical fact behind the test order:** Whisper always pads the input to a **30-second window**, so the encoder costs about the same for a 3 s phrase as for a 30 s one. Turbo shortens only the decoder, and BuzzASR has exactly the large-v3 encoder. **If the large-v3 encoder is too slow on this CPU, the whole Whisper-large family is out for live use**, including the most accurate candidate. That's the cheapest question to answer first. CTC models (MMS) don't have this fixed cost.

- **Status:** Research done. Measurements pending (EXP-01).

## D-006 · EXP-01: Whisper CPU speed and accuracy probe *(proposed)*
- **Question:** On this laptop, how long does Whisper large-v3 / large-v3-turbo (int8, faster-whisper) take per short Armenian phrase, and how accurate is it?
- **Why first:** Cheapest install (one pip package, MIT, no PyTorch). It decides whether BuzzASR is worth converting, or whether we move to CTC models.
- **Inputs:** 3 clips you record yourself (~3 s, ~6 s, ~10 s), Eastern Armenian, one containing an English term, each with typed reference text. Different lengths test whether time grows with length, which feeds the segmentation decision.
- **Fixed settings:** `device=cpu`, `compute_type=int8`, `cpu_threads=4`, `language="hy"`, `vad_filter=False`, beam size 1 and 5, plugged in, Best performance, call app open.
- **Measured:** model load time, transcription time per clip (median of 3 warm runs), real-time factor, peak RAM, CER and WER (normalised).
- **Decision rule** (thresholds from the latency budget in PLAN.md):
  - large-v3 ≤ ~2 s on the 6 s clip → next: convert and test **BuzzASR**.
  - only turbo ≤ ~2 s → judge turbo's accuracy. Is it usable?
  - neither ≤ ~2 s → Whisper-large is out for live use. Next: **MMS-1b-all**.
- **Status:** Proposed. Nothing installed or downloaded.
````

I checked the speech-recognition candidates and wrote the results to a new `DECISIONS.md` in your folder. I also added your answers to `PLAN.md`. Nothing is installed or downloaded.

**I couldn't verify Python or Git on Windows.** The shell I can use on your laptop runs in a Linux virtual machine that only sees your project folder (it reports Python 3.10 on Linux), so it can't see your Windows setup. Please run these in PowerShell and paste the output:

```powershell
python --version
py -0p
where.exe python
python -c "import platform, struct; print(platform.platform(), struct.calcsize('P')*8, 'bit')"
git --version
```

We need 64-bit Python, because the libraries the models run on only publish ready-made Windows builds for 64-bit.

**What the checks found:**
- **Whisper large-v3 and its faster "turbo" version:** both support Armenian, are MIT-licensed, and install natively on Windows with one package (`faster-whisper`), without PyTorch. Without Armenian training, large-v3 gets about 15% of characters wrong. Turbo's Armenian quality is unknown.
- **BuzzASR/armenian:** the most accurate option on paper, at about 2.3% of characters wrong (its own figure), MIT-licensed. It only comes in a format the fast Whisper library can't load directly. Its vocabulary also differs from standard Whisper (53,474 tokens vs 51,866), so converting it is a risk we'd have to test.
- **Meta MMS-1b-all:** Armenian support is confirmed and it runs on Windows. Its licence is non-commercial only, which is fine for the challenge.
- **Meta Omnilingual ASR:** the official toolkit it depends on has no native Windows support, and I couldn't confirm it handles Armenian. I've put it aside.
- **Small community Whisper models trained for Armenian:** they report 40–75% of words wrong, so I dropped them.

**Why the order matters:** Whisper pads every input to a 30-second window. So its first stage (the encoder) costs about the same for a 3-second phrase as for a 30-second one. Turbo only speeds up the second stage, and BuzzASR has exactly the large-v3 encoder. If that encoder is too slow on your processor, the whole large Whisper family is out for live use, including the most accurate model. MMS doesn't have this fixed cost: it works only on the actual audio length.

**Proposed first experiment:** time and score Whisper large-v3 and turbo on your laptop.
- **Install:** a virtual environment with `faster-whisper`, `jiwer` (for error rates) and `psutil` (for memory). Then download two models, about 4.5 GB.
- **Your recordings:** three clips of Eastern Armenian, about 3, 6 and 10 seconds long, each with the exact text typed out, and one including an English term. Windows Sound Recorder is enough, since `faster-whisper` reads its files directly. The different lengths show whether processing time grows with phrase length, which feeds into how we split long phrases.
- **Measurements:** time per clip, memory use, and the share of characters and words wrong, with the laptop plugged in, Best performance mode on, and a call app open.
- **What decides the next step**, using about 2 seconds for the 6-second clip as the limit:
  - If large-v3 stays under it, we convert and test BuzzASR.
  - If only turbo does, we look at whether turbo's accuracy is usable.
  - If neither does, we move to MMS.

My guess is that large-v3 will be too slow on this processor, but it's only a guess. The test is cheap and settles it with a number we can show in the interview.

If this looks right to you, send the PowerShell output and record the three clips. I'll then write the small test script for you to read before we install anything.

Sources:
- [BuzzASR/armenian model card](https://huggingface.co/BuzzASR/armenian)
- [BuzzASR paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.09554)
- [faster-whisper on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/faster-whisper/1.0.0)
- [faster-whisper discussion on 30-second padding](https://github.com/SYSTRAN/faster-whisper/discussions/837)
- [MMS-1b-all ONNX (licence, Armenian pack)](https://huggingface.co/OpenVoiceOS/mms-1b-all-onnx)

- [Omnilingual ASR guide](https://soniqo.audio/guides/omnilingual)
- [Edmon02/whisper-small-hy](https://friendli.ai/models/Edmon02/whisper-small-hy)

````
README.md
convert_all_omni_to_hf.py
requirements.txt
# omnilingual_to_hf

Convert all OmniASR models from [fairseq2](https://github.com/facebookresearch/fairseq2)
format to [HuggingFace](https://huggingface.co/) `Wav2Vec2ForCTC` checkpoints, and
optionally push them to the HuggingFace Hub.

---

## What this does

OmniASR is a family of multilingual CTC speech recognition models trained at four scales
(300M · 1B · 3B · 7B) across two generations (v1 CTC / v2 CTC).  They are distributed
through the `fairseq2` model hub as part of the `omnilingual_asr` package.

This repository provides a single self-contained script — `convert_all_omni_to_hf.py` —
that:

1. Loads each OmniASR variant from the fairseq2 hub.
2. **Auto-detects** all architecture parameters (layer count, hidden size, FFN width,
   attention heads, vocab size) directly from the model's state dict — no hardcoded
   lookup tables.
3. Writes a complete HuggingFace tokenizer bundle (`vocab.json`,
   `tokenizer_config.json`, `special_tokens_map.json`, `preprocessor_config.json`)
   from the fairseq2 SentencePiece vocabulary.
4. Converts all model weights using a verified fairseq2 → HF key mapping.
5. **Validates parity**: decodes the same audio file with both the original fairseq2
   model and the converted HF model, then compares logits, greedy token IDs, and
   decoded transcripts — all while both models are still in memory.
6. Saves the HF checkpoint locally.
7. Pushes to the HuggingFace Hub (optional).

### Models covered

| Tag | fairseq2 card | HF repo |
|-----|---------------|---------|
| v1 300M | `omniASR_CTC_300M` | `{user}/omniASR-CTC-300M` |
| v1 1B   | `omniASR_CTC_1B`   | `{user}/omniASR-CTC-1B`   |
| v1 3B   | `omniASR_CTC_3B`   | `{user}/omniASR-CTC-3B`   |
| v1 7B   | `omniASR_CTC_7B`   | `{user}/omniASR-CTC-7B`   |
| v2 300M | `omniASR_CTC_300M_v2` | `{user}/omniASR-CTC-300M-v2` |
| v2 1B   | `omniASR_CTC_1B_v2`   | `{user}/omniASR-CTC-1B-v2`   |
| v2 3B   | `omniASR_CTC_3B_v2`   | `{user}/omniASR-CTC-3B-v2`   |
| v2 7B   | `omniASR_CTC_7B_v2`   | `{user}/omniASR-CTC-7B-v2`   |

Both v1 and v2 use the wav2vec2-v2 feature extractor (per-layer layer norm on all 7
conv layers).  Architecture dimensions are detected at runtime from the state dict.

---

## Prerequisites

### 1 — omnilingual conda environment

The script must run inside the `omnilingual` conda environment where `fairseq2` and
`omnilingual_asr` are installed (these are not on PyPI):

```bash
conda activate omnilingual
pip install torch torchaudio transformers huggingface_hub
```

### 2 — fairseq2 asset directory

Point fairseq2 at the local asset store that contains the OmniASR model cards:

```bash
export FAIRSEQ2_ASSETS_DIR=/path/to/omnilingual/fairseq2_assets
```

---

## HuggingFace authentication

You need a HuggingFace account and a token with **write** permissions.
Generate one at https://huggingface.co/settings/tokens.

**Option A — environment variable (recommended for scripts):**

```bash
export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
````

```
cat > /tmp/claude-0/-home-claude/6aa59ffb-ae67-5ffa-b0df-64d38a74cb18/scratchpad/estimate.py <<'EOF'
# Back-of-envelope compute estimates (MACs) for ASR candidates on a short phrase.
# Assumptions are printed; results are rough (±2x) and only meant to rank candidates.
PHRASE_S = 6.0          # phrase length (s)
TOKENS = 70             # Whisper output tokens for ~6 s of Armenian (byte-level BPE is inefficient for Armenian)
def whisper(d, enc_layers, dec_layers, vocab=51866, T=1500, mels=128):
    enc = enc_layers * (12*d*d*T + 2*T*T*d) + mels*d*3*3000 + d*d*3*T
    cross_kv = dec_layers * 2*d*d*T                     # computed once per call
    per_tok = dec_layers * 14*d*d + d*vocab
    dec_params_bytes = per_tok                          # int8: ~1 byte per weight read per token
    return enc, cross_kv + per_tok*TOKENS, dec_params_bytes
def w2v_ctc(d, layers, ff_mult=4, vocab=10288, sec=PHRASE_S):
    T = int(50*sec)
    cnn = 2.45e9*sec
    tr = layers*((4+2*ff_mult)*d*d*T + 2*T*T*d)
    pos = d*(d/16)*128*T
    return cnn + tr + pos + d*vocab*T
rows = []
for name, args in [("Whisper large-v3 / BuzzASR", (1280,32,32)), ("Whisper large-v3-turbo", (1280,32,4)), ("Whisper medium", (1024,24,24)), ("Whisper small", (768,12,12))]:
    e, dcd, bpt = whisper(*args)
    rows.append((name, e, dcd, bpt))
for name, args in [("MMS-1b-all / omniASR-CTC-1B", (1280,48)), ("omniASR-CTC-300M", (1024,24))]:
    rows.append((name, w2v_ctc(*args), 0, 0))
print(f"phrase={PHRASE_S}s, whisper tokens={TOKENS}")
for GOPS in (150e9, 300e9):
    print(f"\n-- effective throughput {GOPS/1e9:.0f} GMAC/s (int8, 4 cores; pessimistic/optimistic) --")
    for name, e, dcd, bpt in rows:
        t_compute = (e+dcd)/GOPS
        # greedy decoding is memory-bound: weights read once per token, ~15 GB/s effective
        t_mem = bpt*TOKENS/15e9
        print(f"{name:30s} encoder/body {e/1e9:6.0f} GMAC  decoder {dcd/1e9:5.0f} GMAC  ~{t_compute+t_mem:5.1f} s")
EOF
python3 /tmp/claude-0/-home-claude/6aa59ffb-ae67-5ffa-b0df-64d38a74cb18/scratchpad/estimate.py
```

```
## D-007 · Compute estimate per phrase on the i5-8250U *(back-of-envelope, to be measured)*

Method: count multiply-accumulates (MACs) from each architecture for one **6 s phrase**, and assume ~70 Whisper output tokens. Armenian is token-inefficient in Whisper's byte-level vocabulary. Then divide by an assumed **effective** throughput of 150–300 GMAC/s (4 cores, int8, AVX2, 15 W under sustained load). Greedy decoding is limited by memory bandwidth, so it's estimated separately at ~15 GB/s. Treat these as ±2×. They are for **ranking**, not promises.

| Model | Work per 6 s phrase | Est. ASR time | Est. RAM (int8 / fp32) | Download |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Whisper large-v3 / BuzzASR | ~1,350 GMAC (encoder alone ~1,140, **fixed** because of the 30 s window) | **~8–13 s** | ~2 GB / — | 3.1 GB |
| Whisper large-v3-turbo | ~1,170 GMAC (same encoder) | **~4.5–8.5 s** | ~1.2 GB / — | 1.6 GB |
| Whisper medium | ~670 GMAC | ~4–6.5 s | ~1 GB / — | 1.5 GB |
| Whisper small | ~200 GMAC | ~1.3–2 s | ~0.5 GB / — | 0.5 GB (but Armenian accuracy is poor) |
| MMS-1b-all / omniASR-CTC-1B | ~320 GMAC (**scales with phrase length**) | ~1–2 s int8, ~3 s fp32 | ~1.2 GB / ~4 GB | 3.7–3.9 GB |
| **omniASR-CTC-300M-v2** | ~115 GMAC (scales with length) | **~0.4–0.8 s** int8, ~1.2 s fp32 | ~0.4 GB / ~1.3 GB | **1.3 GB** |

One external data point for scale: on 6 Apple M1 Max CPU cores (faster than this laptop), faster-whisper int8 ran large-v3 at about real time and turbo about 3.2× faster on a 5-minute file *(classmethod.jp)*.

**Reading of the table:**
- With an unmodified 30-second window, the **whole Whisper-large family**, including the most accurate model (BuzzASR), is predicted to need **more than the 5 s total budget for ASR alone**. Turbo is borderline even in the optimistic case.
- The CTC models fit the budget. The 300M model leaves room for translation, speaker ID and two speakers finishing at once.

**Trade-offs of CTC models to keep in mind:**
- They probably output no punctuation and no casing, which may hurt translation.
- English words probably come out as Armenian-script spellings, or wrong.
- The Armenian accuracy of the small CTC models isn't published.

A possible later rescue for Whisper is whisper.cpp's `audio_ctx` option, which shrinks the encoder window to the phrase length. Its quality impact is **unverified**, and we only look at it if the CTC accuracy isn't good enough.

## D-006 · EXP-01 (first version): Whisper CPU speed and accuracy probe *(superseded by D-008)*
```

```
## D-008 · Revised first experiment *(proposed, waiting for agreement)*

**Step 0: CPU calibration (no model download, only `numpy`, ~15 MB).** Run a 60-second sustained matrix-multiply load to measure this laptop's real throughput when plugged in, in Best performance mode and warm. - **Why this model first:**

  - It has an Apache-2.0 licence and confirmed Armenian training data.
  - It runs natively on Windows through `transformers`.
- **Install:** `torch` (CPU-only wheel), `transformers`, `soundfile`, `jiwer` (error rates), `psutil` (RAM). PyTorch is the largest install (~200 MB wheel, ~1 GB on disk).
- **Inputs:** 3 clips (~3 s, ~6 s, ~10 s), 16 kHz mono WAV, Eastern Armenian, one containing an English technical term, each with exact reference text.
- **Measured:** model load time; ASR time per clip (median of 3 warm runs) to check that time grows with length; peak RAM; CER and WER (normalised: no punctuation, lowercase); a look at the raw output for punctuation and how English words come out.
- **Decision rule:**
  - CER good enough and English readable after translation → keep 300M and move on to translation (M4).
  - Fast but inaccurate → EXP-02: omniASR-CTC-1B-v2 (3.7 GB, ~1–2 s estimated) or MMS-1b-all as a cross-check.
  - Both CTC models inaccurate → revisit Whisper with a shrunk encoder window (D-007).
- **Status:** Proposed.
```

Your environment is fine. The one catch is that `python` opens the Microsoft Store, so we'll create the virtual environment with `py -3.12 -m venv .venv` and use `.venv\Scripts\python` after that.

**The comparison changed my recommendation.** Last time I suggested testing Whisper large-v3 and Turbo first. Once I worked out how much computation each model needs per phrase, that looked like a 1.6–4.6 GB download just to confirm that Whisper is too slow. These figures are rough estimates from each model's architecture, not measurements:

| Model | Estimated speech-recognition time for a 6 s phrase | RAM | Download |
|---|---|---|---|
| Whisper large-v3 / BuzzASR | ~8–13 s | ~2 GB | 3.1 GB |
| Whisper large-v3-turbo | ~4.5–8.5 s | ~1.2 GB | 1.6 GB |
| MMS-1b-all / Omnilingual CTC-1B | ~1–2 s, or ~3 s without int8 compression | ~1.2–4 GB | 3.7–3.9 GB |
| **Omnilingual CTC-300M** | **~0.4–1.2 s** | ~0.4–1.3 GB | **1.3 GB** |

- **Why Whisper looks too slow:** it always processes a 30-second window, even for a 3-second phrase. Turbo and BuzzASR use the same large encoder, so they have the same fixed cost. Only the decoding step is lighter.
- **Why the CTC models look fast:** they process only the actual length of the audio, in a single pass.
- **Outside data point:** on 6 Apple M1 Max cores, which are faster than yours, large-v3 ran at about real time and Turbo about 3× faster ([classmethod.jp](https://dev.classmethod.jp/articles/openai-whisper-large-v3-turbo-faster-whisper/)).

I treat the estimates as accurate only to within about 2×. They're good for ranking the models, not as promises.

**New finding: Omnilingual supports Armenian.** I checked Meta's repository directly. `hye_Armn` (Eastern Armenian) is in the language list, with 294 hours of Armenian training data. Meta reports 1.9% of characters wrong for its largest model; there's no Armenian figure for the small 300M model. The official toolkit doesn't run on Windows, but a community conversion to the standard Hugging Face format exists. Its conversion script compares the converted model's outputs with the original's.

**Proposed first experiment:**
1. **Measure your processor's real speed (no model download).** A 60-second load test using only `numpy`, a 15 MB package, with the laptop plugged in and warm. This replaces my assumed speed with a measured one. If your laptop turns out much faster than I assumed, Turbo comes back into the test.
2. **Test Omnilingual CTC-300M on your three clips** (about 3, 6 and 10 seconds). Download: 1.3 GB, plus PyTorch for CPU, about 1 GB installed. We measure time per clip, peak memory and the share of characters and words wrong. We also look at the raw output: does it have punctuation, and how do English words come out?

**The trade-offs to accept:**
- CTC models probably output no punctuation, which may make translation worse.
- English terms will probably come out as Armenian-script spellings or errors. Whisper handles mixed languages better.
- Nobody has published accuracy for the small model, which is the reason to test it.

If it's fast but not accurate enough, the next step is the 1B version (3.7 GB). If both CTC models disappoint, we look again at Whisper with a shorter processing window. I've written all of this into `DECISIONS.md` (sections D-007 and D-008).

**Do you agree with starting with the processor speed test, then Omnilingual CTC-300M?** If yes, I'll write the two small scripts for you to read before anything is installed.

```
# Claude Code agent proxy

Outbound HTTPS from this session goes through a local proxy at http://127.0.0.1:43045
(set via HTTPS_PROXY) which tunnels to a policy-enforcing egress proxy. TLS is
re-terminated there, so every tool must trust the CA bundle at
/root/.ccr/ca-bundle.crt. The standard CA environment variables, the system trust
store (where possible), a JVM truststore, the Bazel system bazelrc, the
browser NSS store, and gsutil's boto config are already set up.

## Quick diagnosis

1. Run: curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:43045/__agentproxy/status
   It reports proxy state, which trust and git accommodations are active
   (javaTrustStorePath, toolTrustFailureCodes, gitSshRewrite,
   gitConfigConflicts), and the most recent proxy-side failures.
2. Find the failure class below and apply the matching fix; gitConfigConflicts
   codes map to the git section, toolTrustFailureCodes to the JVM section.
3. Never disable TLS verification, never unset HTTPS_PROXY, and do not retry
   policy denials (403/407) — report them instead.

## Failure classes and fixes

### "certificate verify failed" / "self-signed certificate in chain" / PKIX errors

The failing tool is not reading the pre-set CA configuration. In order:

- If the tool has a CA flag or env var, point it at /root/.ccr/ca-bundle.crt
  (examples: --cacert, SSL_CERT_FILE, NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE,
  AWS_CA_BUNDLE, DENO_CERT, CARGO_HTTP_CAINFO, PIP_CERT, GIT_SSL_CAINFO,
  BUNDLE_SSL_CA_CERT, HEX_CACERTS_PATH, NIX_SSL_CERT_FILE).
- Tool config files override environment variables. If one of these sets its
  own CA or disables verification, point it at the bundle instead:
  pip.conf "cert", npm "cafile" (npm config get cafile), ~/.curlrc "cacert",
  .wgetrc "ca_certificate", conda "ssl_verify", git "http.sslCAInfo",
  gradle.properties / MAVEN_OPTS "-Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore".
- JVM tools (Maven, Gradle, plain Java): when a JDK is present,
  JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS points JVMs at a truststore that holds the proxy CA: the
  JDK's own store if the system trust install already added the CA there,
  otherwise /root/.ccr/java-truststore.p12 (password "changeit"). Confirm
  javaTrustStorePath is set in the status output before pointing a build at it
  (toolTrustFailureCodes explains why it is missing). If the image or the
  build sets its own trustStore, that one wins — import the proxy CA into it
  with
  keytool -importcert -noprompt -alias ccr-agent-proxy -file /root/.ccr/agent-proxy-ca.crt -keystore <their store>
  or point the build at the ready-made one. Bazel reads the managed block in
  /etc/bazel.bazelrc rather than JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS.

### "405 Method Not Allowed" from the proxy

The tool sent a plain-HTTP (non-CONNECT) request: usually axios older than
1.16.1 (upgrade it) or a tool configured with HTTP_PROXY (unset HTTP_PROXY for
that tool — only HTTPS_PROXY is supported).

### 403 / 407 from the proxy

Most often the destination host is not allowed for this session. Do not retry
or route around it — report the blocked host.
Note: curl hides response bodies on failed CONNECTs; the status endpoint
records the reason.
```

```
"""Back-of-envelope compute cost of the ASR candidates.

Counts multiply-accumulate operations (MACs) from each model's architecture
for one phrase of a given length. 1 MAC = 2 FLOPs.

These numbers are for *ranking* candidates and for turning a measured CPU
throughput into a rough time prediction. They are not a substitute for timing
the real model (see DECISIONS.md, D-007).

Assumptions are written next to the code so they can be challenged.
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass

# Whisper always pads its input to a 30 s window = 1500 encoder positions.
WHISPER_ENCODER_POSITIONS = 1500
WHISPER_MEL_FRAMES = 3000
# ASSUMPTION: ~12 output tokens per second of Armenian speech. Whisper's
# byte-level vocabulary has few Armenian merges, so Armenian needs many tokens.
WHISPER_TOKENS_PER_SECOND = 12

# wav2vec2-style CTC models (MMS, Omnilingual) produce one frame per 20 ms.
CTC_FRAMES_PER_SECOND = 50
# The 7-layer convolutional feature extractor costs ~2.45 GMAC per second of
# 16 kHz audio (computed from its layer shapes: 512 channels, strides 5,2,2,2,2,2,2).
CTC_CNN_MACS_PER_SECOND = 2.45e9


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class WhisperArch:
    name: str
    d_model: int
    encoder_layers: int
    decoder_layers: int
    n_mels: int = 128
    vocab: int = 51866


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CtcArch:
    name: str
    d_model: int
    layers: int
    vocab: int
    ffn_mult: int = 4


WHISPER_MODELS = [
    WhisperArch("Whisper large-v3 / BuzzASR", 1280, 32, 32),
    WhisperArch("Whisper large-v3-turbo", 1280, 32, 4),
    WhisperArch("Whisper medium", 1024, 24, 24, n_mels=80),
    WhisperArch("Whisper small", 768, 12, 12, n_mels=80),
]

CTC_MODELS = [
    CtcArch("omniASR-CTC-1B / MMS-1b-all", 1280, 48, vocab=10288),
    CtcArch("omniASR-CTC-300M", 1024, 24, vocab=10288),
]


def _transformer_layer_macs(d: int, positions: int, ffn_mult: int = 4) -> float:
    """One transformer layer: Q/K/V/O projections + feed-forward + attention."""
    projections = 4 * d * d * positions
    feed_forward = 2 * ffn_mult * d * d * positions
    attention = 2 * positions * positions * d
    return projections + feed_forward + attention


def whisper_costs(arch: WhisperArch, phrase_seconds: float) -> dict:
    """Return encoder MACs, decoder MACs and bytes read per token (int8 weights).

    The encoder cost does NOT depend on phrase length (fixed 30 s window).
    """
    d, t = arch.d_model, WHISPER_ENCODER_POSITIONS
    conv_stem = arch.n_mels * d * 3 * WHISPER_MEL_FRAMES + d * d * 3 * t
    encoder = arch.encoder_layers * _transformer_layer_macs(d, t) + conv_stem

    tokens = WHISPER_TOKENS_PER_SECOND * phrase_seconds
    cross_attention_kv = arch.decoder_layers * 2 * d * d * t  # once per call
    per_token = arch.decoder_layers * 14 * d * d + d * arch.vocab
    decoder = cross_attention_kv + per_token * tokens

    return {
        "encoder_macs": encoder,
        "decoder_macs": decoder,
        "tokens": tokens,
        # Greedy decoding at batch size 1 reads (roughly) every decoder weight
        # once per token, so it is limited by memory bandwidth, not compute.
        "decoder_bytes_per_token_int8": per_token,
    }


def ctc_costs(arch: CtcArch, phrase_seconds: float) -> dict:
    """Return total MACs for a CTC model. Cost grows with phrase length."""
    d = arch.d_model
    frames = int(CTC_FRAMES_PER_SECOND * phrase_seconds)
    cnn = CTC_CNN_MACS_PER_SECOND * phrase_seconds
    transformer = arch.layers * _transformer_layer_macs(d, frames, arch.ffn_mult)
    positional_conv = d * (d / 16) * 128 * frames  # grouped conv, kernel 128, 16 groups
    output_head = d * arch.vocab * frames
    return {"total_macs": cnn + transformer + positional_conv + output_head}


def predict_seconds(macs_per_second: float, bytes_per_second: float, phrase_seconds: float) -> list[dict]:
    """Predict ASR time per phrase from a measured throughput and memory bandwidth."""
    rows = []
    for arch in WHISPER_MODELS:
        c = whisper_costs(arch, phrase_seconds)
        compute_s = (c["encoder_macs"] + c["decoder_macs"]) / macs_per_second
        memory_s = c["decoder_bytes_per_token_int8"] * c["tokens"] / bytes_per_second
        rows.append({
            "model": arch.name,
            "gmacs": round((c["encoder_macs"] + c["decoder_macs"]) / 1e9),
            "seconds": round(compute_s + memory_s, 2),
            "scales_with_length": False,
        })
    for arch in CTC_MODELS:
        c = ctc_costs(arch, phrase_seconds)
        rows.append({
            "model": arch.name,
            "gmacs": round(c["total_macs"] / 1e9),
            "seconds": round(c["total_macs"] / macs_per_second, 2),
            "scales_with_length": True,
        })
    return rows
```

`content` (raw text):

```
"""CPU calibration benchmark (EXP-00).

Measures this laptop's *sustained* matrix-multiply throughput and memory
bandwidth, then predicts ASR time per phrase for each candidate model using
benchmarks/model_costs.py.

No models are downloaded. The only dependency is numpy.

Usage (from the project folder, inside the venv):
    .venv\\Scripts\\python benchmarks\\cpu_benchmark.py
    .venv\\Scripts\\python benchmarks\\cpu_benchmark.py --duration 60 --threads 4

Results are printed and saved as JSON in results/.
"""

import argparse
import json
import os
import platform
import subprocess
import sys
import time
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path


def parse_args() -> argparse.Namespace:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__, formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)
    p.add_argument("--duration", type=float, default=60.0, help="seconds of sustained load (default 60)")
    p.add_argument("--threads", type=int, default=None, help="BLAS threads (default: library default, usually all logical cores)")
    p.add_argument("--out", type=Path, default=Path("results"), help="folder for the JSON result")
    return p.parse_args()


args = parse_args()
# Thread count must be set BEFORE numpy is imported, otherwise it is ignored.
if args.threads:
    for var in ("OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS", "OMP_NUM_THREADS", "MKL_NUM_THREADS"):
        os.environ[var] = str(args.threads)

import numpy as np  # noqa: E402

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent))
from model_costs import predict_seconds  # noqa: E402


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- system info
def windows_power_info() -> dict:
    """AC/battery state and active power scheme (Windows only)."""
    import ctypes

    class SYSTEM_POWER_STATUS(ctypes.Structure):
        _fields_ = [("ACLineStatus", ctypes.c_ubyte), ("BatteryFlag", ctypes.c_ubyte),
                    ("BatteryLifePercent", ctypes.c_ubyte), ("SystemStatusFlag", ctypes.c_ubyte),
                    ("BatteryLifeTime", ctypes.c_ulong), ("BatteryFullLifeTime", ctypes.c_ulong)]

    status = SYSTEM_POWER_STATUS()
    if not ctypes.windll.kernel32.GetSystemPowerStatus(ctypes.byref(status)):
        raise OSError("GetSystemPowerStatus failed")
    ac = {0: "battery", 1: "plugged in"}.get(status.ACLineStatus, "unknown")
    scheme = subprocess.run(["powercfg", "/getactivescheme"], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip()
    return {"power_source": ac, "power_scheme": scheme}


def total_ram_gb() -> float:
    if sys.platform == "win32":
        import ctypes

        class MEMORYSTATUSEX(ctypes.Structure):
            _fields_ = [("dwLength", ctypes.c_ulong), ("dwMemoryLoad", ctypes.c_ulong),
                        ("ullTotalPhys", ctypes.c_ulonglong), ("ullAvailPhys", ctypes.c_ulonglong),
                        ("ullTotalPageFile", ctypes.c_ulonglong), ("ullAvailPageFile", ctypes.c_ulonglong),
                        ("ullTotalVirtual", ctypes.c_ulonglong), ("ullAvailVirtual", ctypes.c_ulonglong),
                        ("ullAvailExtendedVirtual", ctypes.c_ulonglong)]

        m = MEMORYSTATUSEX()
        m.dwLength = ctypes.sizeof(MEMORYSTATUSEX)
        ctypes.windll.kernel32.GlobalMemoryStatusEx(ctypes.byref(m))
        return round(m.ullTotalPhys / 1e9, 1)
    with open("/proc/meminfo") as f:
        return round(int(f.readline().split()[1]) / 1e6, 1)


def system_info() -> dict:
    info = {
        "timestamp": datetime.now().isoformat(timespec="seconds"),
        "platform": platform.platform(),
        "processor": platform.processor(),
        "logical_cores": os.cpu_count(),
        "ram_gb": total_ram_gb(),
        "python": sys.version.split()[0],
        "numpy": np.__version__,
        "blas_threads_requested": args.threads or "default",
    }
    if sys.platform == "win32":
        info.update(windows_power_info())
    return info


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- benchmarks
def sustained_matmul(m: int, k: int, n: int, duration: float) -> list[float]:
    """Repeat an (m x k) @ (k x n) float32 matmul for `duration` seconds.

    Returns one GFLOP/s sample per second, so throttling shows up as a drop.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    a = rng.standard_normal((m, k), dtype=np.float32)
    b = rng.standard_normal((k, n), dtype=np.float32)
    flops_per_call = 2.0 * m * k * n

    # Warm-up: lets the CPU boost and BLAS start its threads.
    t_end = time.perf_counter() + 3
    while time.perf_counter() < t_end:
        a @ b

    samples, calls = [], 0
    start = window_start = time.perf_counter()
    while True:
        a @ b
        calls += 1
        now = time.perf_counter()
        if now - window_start >= 1.0:
            samples.append(calls * flops_per_call / (now - window_start) / 1e9)
            print(f"\r  t={now - start:5.0f}s  {samples[-1]:7.1f} GFLOP/s", end="", flush=True)
            calls, window_start = 0, now
        if now - start >= duration:
            break
    print()
    return samples


def memory_bandwidth_gbs(size_mb: int = 256, repeats: int = 10) -> float:
    """Copy a large array repeatedly. Counts bytes read + bytes written."""
    src = np.ones(size_mb * 1024 * 1024 // 8, dtype=np.float64)
    dst = np.empty_like(src)
    np.copyto(dst, src)  # warm-up, page faults
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(repeats):
        np.copyto(dst, src)
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0
    return 2 * src.nbytes * repeats / elapsed / 1e9


def median(xs: list[float]) -> float:
    s = sorted(xs)
    return s[len(s) // 2]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- main
def main() -> None:
    info = system_info()
    print("System:", json.dumps(info, indent=2))
    if info.get("power_source") == "battery":
        print("\nWARNING: running on battery. Results will not match the demo setup.\n")

    print(f"\n[1/3] Sustained float32 matmul, CTC-300M feed-forward shape (300x1024 @ 1024x4096), {args.duration:.0f} s")
    ctc_samples = sustained_matmul(300, 1024, 4096, args.duration)

    print("[2/3] Whisper-large encoder shape (1500x1280 @ 1280x5120), 10 s")
    whisper_samples = sustained_matmul(1500, 1280, 5120, 10)

    print("[3/3] Memory bandwidth (256 MB copy)")
    bandwidth = memory_bandwidth_gbs()

    first = median(ctc_samples[:10])
    last = median(ctc_samples[-20:])
    summary = {
        "ctc_shape_gflops_first10s_median": round(first, 1),
        "ctc_shape_gflops_last20s_median": round(last, 1),
        "ctc_shape_gflops_min": round(min(ctc_samples), 1),
        "sustained_ratio_last_vs_first": round(last / first, 2),
        "whisper_shape_gflops_median": round(median(whisper_samples), 1),
        "memory_bandwidth_gbs": round(bandwidth, 1),
    }

    # Predictions use the SUSTAINED (last 20 s) number: a live call is a sustained load.
    # float32 throughput = what PyTorch uses by default. int8 may be faster; we measure that later.
    macs_per_s = last * 1e9 / 2
    predictions = {f"{s:g}s_phrase": predict_seconds(macs_per_s, bandwidth * 1e9, s) for s in (3, 6, 10)}

    print("\nSummary:", json.dumps(summary, indent=2))
    print("\nPredicted ASR time per phrase (float32, from sustained throughput; rough, +/-2x):")
    print(f"  {'model':32s} {'3 s':>7s} {'6 s':>7s} {'10 s':>7s}")
    for i, row in enumerate(predictions["6s_phrase"]):
        t3, t6, t10 = (predictions[k][i]["seconds"] for k in ("3s_phrase", "6s_phrase", "10s_phrase"))
        print(f"  {row['model']:32s} {t3:6.1f}s {t6:6.1f}s {t10:6.1f}s")

    args.out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    out_file = args.out / f"cpu_benchmark_{datetime.now():%Y%m%d_%H%M%S}.json"
    out_file.write_text(json.dumps({
        "system": info, "summary": summary, "per_second_gflops": [round(x, 1) for x in ctc_samples],
        "predictions": predictions,
    }, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
    print(f"\nSaved: {out_file}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

The CPU benchmark is in your project folder and ready to run. Nothing is installed on your laptop yet.

**I couldn't check the converted model from here.** For this session, PyPI and Hugging Face are blocked both from my workspace and from your laptop's shell. So the compatibility check has to run in your PowerShell (D-009 in `DECISIONS.md`).

I did read the relevant parts of the conversion code:
- **Standard format:** it produces a standard `transformers` speech model with its standard tokenizer, with no custom code.
- **How it was checked:** the converter compares the converted model's outputs with the original model's. But it turns the output into text with its own simple code, not the Hugging Face decoding. We'll use the same simple decoding, so our results match what was checked.

**What I added to your folder:**
- `benchmarks/cpu_benchmark.py` runs matrix multiplications the same size as the 300M model's layers, nonstop for 60 seconds, and records speed each second, so any slowdown as the laptop heats up shows. It also measures memory speed, checks you're plugged in, and turns the measured speed into predicted recognition times. Results are saved as JSON in `results/`.
- `benchmarks/model_costs.py` holds the cost calculations from D-007, with each assumption written next to the code.
- `EXPERIMENTS.md` is the log for speed, accuracy and memory, one row per run.
- `requirements-bench.txt` lists only numpy.
- `.gitignore` keeps model weights, audio and the virtual environment out of git.

I ran the script here to make sure it works. The numbers from this 2-core cloud machine don't count.

**How to run it.** First plug in, turn on Best performance, and close heavy apps. Then in PowerShell:

```powershell
cd $HOME\Desktop\Mathrix-Claude-Project

# optional but recommended: first commit
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Plan, decision log, CPU benchmark"

# virtual environment (avoids the Microsoft Store 'python' alias)
py -3.12 -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\python -m pip install --upgrade pip
.venv\Scripts\python -m pip install -r requirements-bench.txt

# run 1: default threads (~75 s, don't use the laptop meanwhile)
.venv\Scripts\python benchmarks\cpu_benchmark.py

# run 2: 4 threads, one per physical core
.venv\Scripts\python benchmarks\cpu_benchmark.py --threads 4
```

There's no need to activate the virtual environment: calling `.venv\Scripts\python` directly avoids PowerShell's script restrictions.

**How to read the results:**
- **Sustained ratio** is the speed in the last 20 seconds divided by the speed in the first 10. Below about 0.8 means the laptop slows down under load, and that's what a live call will see.
- **The prediction table** shows the expected recognition time for 3-, 6- and 10-second phrases. A real model runs somewhat slower than pure matrix multiplication, so these are a best case. That's why the next step times the real model structure.
- **Comparing the two runs** tells us whether to use 4 or 8 threads.

When both runs finish, tell me and I'll read the result files from `results/` and fill in `EXPERIMENTS.md`. Then I'll write the compatibility check: it confirms the Windows packages exist, builds the 300M model with random weights and times it, all without the 1.3 GB download.

```
< - **Status:** Accepted. Runs after EXP-00.
---
> - **Status:** Proposed.
exit=1
```

`new_string` (raw text):

```
Environment: Windows 10 (19045), Python 3.12.3, numpy 2.5.4, i5-8250U (8 logical cores), 8.4 GB RAM, plugged in. The power scheme reports "Balanced". On Windows 10 the "Best performance" slider sits inside that scheme, so `powercfg` can't show it.

| Date | Threads | GFLOP/s first 10 s | GFLOP/s last 20 s (sustained) | Min GFLOP/s | Sustained ratio | Whisper-shape GFLOP/s | Mem. bandwidth GB/s | Raw file |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-10-26 | default (8) | 115.6 | 128.4 | **32.6** | 1.11 | 174.9 | 8.3 | `results/cpu_benchmark_20261026_000640.json` |
| 2026-10-26 | **4** | **169.8** | **144.8** | 114.6 | 0.85 | 135.8 | 10.6 | `results/cpu_benchmark_20261026_000822.json` |

Predicted float32 ASR time per phrase, using the **4-thread sustained** throughput (≈ 72 GMAC/s):

| Model | 3 s | 6 s | 10 s | Fits a ~2 s ASR budget? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Whisper large-v3 / BuzzASR | 21.0 s | 24.1 s | 28.2 s | No |
| Whisper large-v3-turbo | 16.6 s | 17.2 s | 18.0 s | No |
| Whisper medium | 10.5 s | 12.1 s | 14.2 s | No |
| Whisper small | 3.2 s | 3.8 s | 4.5 s | No |
| omniASR-CTC-1B / MMS-1b-all | 2.2 s | 4.4 s | 7.5 s | Only short phrases |
| **omniASR-CTC-300M** | **0.8 s** | **1.6 s** | **2.7 s** | **Yes, up to ~7 s phrases** |

### Findings
1. **Use 4 threads (one per physical core), not the default 8.** With 8 threads, throughput swung between 33 and 155 GFLOP/s, with several drops below 50. With 4 threads it stayed between 115 and 172. For a live system, **stable latency matters more than peak speed.** The likely cause is two threads competing for one physical core (hyper-threading), plus background tasks.
2. **Moderate throttling under sustained load.** With 4 threads, speed dropped from ~170 to ~145 GFLOP/s (ratio 0.85). Predictions use the sustained number, since a call is a sustained load.
3. **Memory bandwidth is low: 8–11 GB/s.** I assumed ~15 GB/s. This suggests a single-channel RAM configuration (to be confirmed). It hurts autoregressive decoders like Whisper's, and large models in general. One more reason against Whisper-large.
4. **My earlier estimate (D-007) was optimistic by roughly 2–4×.** It assumed 150–300 GMAC/s (int8). The measured float32 rate is ~72 GMAC/s. The conclusion holds and is now stronger: **only CTC-300M fits comfortably.** CTC-1B fits only for short phrases, unless int8 helps a lot.
5. **Caveat:** these are pure matrix-multiply numbers, a best case. A real model also spends time in convolutions, attention, normalisation and Python overhead. The compatibility check (CHK-01) measures the real 300M architecture.
```

<details><summary>Tool call: <code>Write</code></summary>

<sub>tool_use id `toolu_01RDQYBKNd8xna6RvuqJ8ww8`</sub>
