  - HANDOVER.md is marked as historical.

- **DECISIONS.md** has a new entry, **D-037**.
- **`benchmarks/exp02_mt_eval.py`**: one comment notes that float32 needs the new flag.

**1. Commit** (in the project folder):
```powershell
git add -A
git commit -m "D-037: float32 NLLB conversion optional; README/HANDOVER updates"
git status
```

**2. Fresh-clone test** in a new folder next to the project:
```powershell
cd C:\Users\Hasmik\Desktop
git clone Mathrix-Claude-Project Mathrix-clone-test
cd Mathrix-clone-test

```

Notes on the steps:

Running it twice did no harm, and the install from the clone works. The latency did not pass this time, though, so I want one quick check before the final test.

**Was the double run a problem?** No. The first run (18:13) lasted under a minute, captured only the mic and played no call audio. It had stopped before the second run started at 18:20, so the two never competed for the CPU.

**Fresh clone: passed.**
- The clone is at the latest commit (`b5fd9f7`), and everything installed from the README.
- The 3 models are in place; float32 was correctly left out.
- The app loaded and captured both sides with no lost audio.
- The speaker prior from `assets/` worked.
- Seen from my side, git marks every file as changed. That's almost certainly just Windows line endings. Please run `git status` in PowerShell in the clone folder; it should say "nothing to commit" apart from the two new logs.

**Latency: not passing, and it's not the code.**
- 9 of 17 lines were over 5 s, max 6.3 s. Before today, the worst we'd measured was 1 line over 5 s in each of LIVE-02 and LIVE-04a. The clone runs exactly the same code with the same settings.
- The log shows why. Phrases didn't wait in a queue; each model was simply slower than before:

| Step | Earlier runs | This run |
|---|---|---|
| Translation | median 0.44 s, max 1.2 s | **0.8–2.1 s** |
| Speech recognition, ~7 s phrase | ~2.8 s | **3.3–3.7 s** |

That pattern means something else was using the CPU. Likely causes, which I can't see from here:
- the laptop on battery, or not in Best performance mode;
- Windows Defender or Search scanning the 4 GB of models and the new venv that were just copied;
- the browser playing the video.

**Your speech:** your sentences were recognised well (confidence 0.92–0.95). Two very short sounds were shown as "unclear", as designed.

**Speakers:** the video produced Speaker 1 for 3 lines, then Speaker 2. How many people were talking in that video? If it was one person, that's the occasional extra speaker already listed in the README limitations.

**Next step (a check, not a change):**
1. Confirm the laptop is plugged in and set to Best performance, and close other apps. Wait a few minutes so Defender can finish scanning.
2. Run the same video for about 1 minute in the **original** project folder:

The clone test passes: the slowdown came from the laptop's conditions, not the clone. One borderline issue is left: 3 of 19 lines took slightly over 5 s.

**Clone vs original:** this run in the original folder is as fast as before, and the clone run was about 40 % slower in both models:

| | ASR, phrases ≥ 6 s | Translation, median | Lines over 5 s |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mon, LIVE-04a (original folder) | 2.3 s | 0.96 s | 1 / 23 |
| **Today, original folder** | **2.3 s** | **0.85 s** | **3 / 19** |
| Today, clone (just after copying 4 GB) | 3.4 s | 1.6 s | 9 / 17 |

The code is identical, so the clone itself isn't the cause. The likely cause is that the clone ran right after the install, while Windows was probably still scanning or indexing the new files and the laptop's power mode may have been different. For the demo, that means: run once beforehand, wait a few minutes after any install, and keep the laptop plugged in on Best performance. I'll add this to the README.

**The remaining issue: 3 of 19 lines over 5 s.** They're over by 0.01, 0.06 and 0.46 s. In all three:
- the phrase came from the video and was long (5.5–6.6 s) and densely spoken;
- translation took longer than usual (1.1–1.7 s);
- nothing was waiting in a queue.

So this is the plain processing cost of a long phrase, and it's the same level as Monday (5.2 s max). The earlier tests that had no lines over 5 s had shorter phrases. In a real call, turns are usually shorter than a monologue in a video. Your own lines were all under 4 s.

There are two options, and the choice is yours:
- **A. Accept and document it honestly.** The README and TESTS.md would say: median 4.3 s, about 15 % of long, uninterrupted phrases from the call side at 5.0–5.5 s. No changes to the code.
- **B. One measured experiment:** shorten the maximum phrase length from 7 s to 6 s. That's a single constant (D-014), not new logic.
  - It cuts processing time on long phrases by roughly 0.5 s.
  - The cost: more sentences get cut in the middle, which can hurt the translation.
  - I'd only adopt it if a run with `--record` on the same video shows both fewer lines over 5 s and translations that are no worse.

I lean slightly towards **B**, because ≤ 5 s is a stated requirement and the change is one number we can measure. **A** is defensible if you'd rather freeze the code now. Which do you prefer?

```
**fp32 observations:**

  - `հայերեն` → `հայրեն`.
  - `անգլերեն` → `անգլեր են` (extra space).
  - Without the English term, clip03 CER ≈ 4.7 %.
- **The output is lowercase with no punctuation.** Raw CER is higher only because of capitals and `։`. This matters for translation, which will get unpunctuated lowercase input.
- **Deterministic** (all 3 runs identical), no `<unk>` tokens.
- **Latency is over the ~2 s budget for a 6 s phrase (2.77 s).** Short clips were slower than CHK-01 predicted: clip01 1.92 s vs ~1.4 s scaled, clip02 2.77 s vs ~2.1 s. clip03 matched (3.63 s vs 3.83 s for 10 s). The cause is unknown. To investigate after the int8 run, without guessing.

**fp32 vs int8 comparison:**
1. **Accuracy:** int8 is **+1.0 CER point** worse (6.3 % vs 5.4 %), within the pre-agreed +2 limit. 3 characters changed in total: 2 new errors in clip02, and 1 fixed + 1 new in clip03. Both new errors drop a short word-initial sound or the space before it. That's too few characters to call it a pattern. Watch it as the eval set grows.
2. **Latency:** int8 is **~1.9× faster** with real weights (RTF 0.26 vs 0.46). **6 s phrase: 1.50 s, within the ~2 s ASR budget.** 9.5 s phrase: 2.60 s, over budget. So segments need a cap around **7–8 s** (to be tuned).
3. **Unexpected:** in CHK-01 (random weights) int8 was only 8–25 % faster than fp32. With real weights it's ~1.9× faster. int8 latency matches CHK-01, but **fp32 with real weights is slower than with random weights.** One untested hypothesis is denormal (extremely small) floating-point numbers slowing fp32 arithmetic. It could be tested with `torch.set_flush_denormal(True)`. **Low priority: we use int8.**
4. **RAM:** int8 steady state ≈ **1.0 GB** (RSS at end), vs ≈ 1.7 GB fp32. Peak 2.3 GB **only during startup**, while the fp32 model and its int8 copy coexist. Load time is 40 s vs 17 s. If startup RAM or time becomes a problem, we can save the quantised model once and load it directly. Not needed now.
5. **Limits of this experiment:** 3 clips, 1 speaker, 1 mic, read speech, quiet room. It's a smoke test, not a benchmark. Each CER point here is about 3 characters.
```

```
README
Live Armenian → English call transcription (local, CPU-only)

A Python program that listens to a live call, transcribes spoken Armenian, and prints an English translation in the terminal, labelled by speaker, while the conversation is still running. Everything runs locally on a laptop CPU: no cloud APIs.

Your microphone → Me
System audio (the other side of the call, any app: Zoom, Meet, Telegram, …) → Speaker 1, Speaker 2, …
[00:01:59] Me   (2.8 s)
  HY: այսօր եղանակը շատ լավ է
  EN: Today the weather is very good.
[00:00:39] Speaker 2   (4.9 s)
  HY: բայց ռոբորտ կոչվածի դասական սահմանումը ենձիեն ...
  EN: But the classic definition of a robot is that ...
[00:00:34] Me   (1.6 s)
  HY: ր   (unclear)
  EN: [unclear speech, not translated]

(Format example assembled from lines of recorded test sessions; the speaker number is illustrative.) The number in brackets is the measured latency: from the end of the spoken phrase to the moment the English line is printed.

Target machine (the one used for all measurements): Windows 10 64-bit, Intel Core i5-8250U (4 cores), 8 GB RAM, no GPU, Jabra EVOLVE 20 headset.

1. Setup
1.1 Prerequisites
Windows 10/11, 64-bit. System-audio capture uses WASAPI loopback, which is Windows-only.
Python 3.12, 64-bit (python.org installer). Use the py launcher: on many systems the bare python command opens the Microsoft Store.
Git, ~6 GB free disk (models ~4.5 GB + Python packages), internet for the one-time model download.
A headset. Echo cancellation is out of scope. With loudspeakers, the mic would pick up the call and label it Me.
1.2 Install
git clone <this repository> Mathrix-Claude-Project
cd Mathrix-Claude-Project
py -3.12 -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
.venv\Scripts\python -m unittest discover tests        # 21 unit tests, should end with: OK

All commands call .venv\Scripts\python directly, so there's no need to activate the venv (and no PowerShell script-policy issues).

1.3 Download the models (one time, ~4 GB download)
.venv\Scripts\python tools\download_model.py           # ASR: omniASR-CTC-300M-v2, 1.3 GB, SHA-256 verified
.venv\Scripts\python tools\prepare_nllb.py             # MT: NLLB-200-distilled-600M (2.5 GB) → CTranslate2 int8
.venv\Scripts\python tools\download_speaker_model.py   # speaker embeddings: WeSpeaker ResNet34-LM, 26 MB
Every model is downloaded at a pinned revision and verified against the published SHA-256 where one exists (models/*/REVISION.txt, SOURCE.txt).
prepare_nllb.py converts the official weights locally. Close the browser first: conve
```
